opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about promptable world events is really as a way to give people more control over what happens in the world, beyond just navigating it. With Genie 3, you can move around an environment that's generated in real time, but at some point you want to say, "What if it starts raining here?" or "What if a herd of deer runs across the path?" or "Let's put a different character over there." And the interesting thing is that these events don't just get pasted on top. The model has to integrate them into the world in a way that's consistent with what's already there: the lighting, the physics, the layout of the scene, everything you've seen so far.

So I think of it as a second channel of interaction. One channel is the actions, moving, looking around, the agent or the user acting within the world. The other is this text-based channel where you can change the state of the world itself. That opens up a lot of things. For entertainment and creative exploration, it lets you steer the story. But I'm actually quite excited about it for training agents, because you can create what-if scenarios, counterfactuals, unusual situations that would be really hard or expensive to capture in the real world. You want to see how an agent reacts when something unexpected happens, like an obstacle appearing or the weather changing, and world events give you a natural way to introduce that.

Where it's still early is how fine-grained and reliable that control is, and how long these changes stay consistent as you keep interacting. But the direction is that the world should feel responsive, not just to where you go, but to what you want to happen in it.

r001.rationale: The response describes text-prompted events such as rain or deer crossing the path as changes to the world beyond the agent’s movement, so they need not be caused by the agent.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that prompted content may appear only when the user looks toward another part of the world.

r003.rationale: It says events should be integrated consistently rather than pasted on, but does not describe conditioning the next-frame generation process.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we're really excited about. The way I think about it is that Genie 3 gives you an environment that you can navigate, and that's already a big step, but a world isn't really a world if nothing ever happens in it beyond what you do with the controls. So promptable world events are our way of letting you, or an agent, or whoever is driving the experience, say "and now this happens." You're walking through a street and you prompt "a car drives past," or "it starts raining," or "a character shows up," and the model has to integrate that into the ongoing scene in a way that's consistent with everything it has already generated.

And the key word there is consistent. The thing that makes Genie 3 different from a text-to-video model is that it's interactive and it maintains memory over time. So when you inject an event, it shouldn't feel like the model just cut to a different clip. The rain has to fall on the same buildings you were looking at, the car has to drive on the road that was already there, and if you turn around and come back a minute later, the world should still remember that it happened. That's a hard problem, and honestly it's one of the places where you can see the model still getting things wrong sometimes, but when it works it's pretty magical.

From a use-case perspective, I think of events as a way to introduce counterfactuals. If you're training an agent, you don't just want it to walk around a static world, you want to be able to throw situations at it. What does it do when an obstacle suddenly appears? What does it do when the conditions change? Promptable events let you create those "what if" scenarios on demand, without having to hand-build every one of them. So in that sense, navigation is the baseline interactivity, and events are a second layer of control that sits on top of it, and the two together are what start to make it feel like a real simulator rather than just a rendering.

r001.rationale: The response describes prompting events such as a passing car, rain, or a character appearing, including situations introduced on demand for an agent. These happenings need not be caused by the agent.

r002.rationale: It discusses turning around and returning later, but does not say that prompted content can be revealed by looking toward another part of the world.

r003.rationale: It says events should be integrated consistently into the ongoing scene, but does not describe conditioning next-frame generation or distinguish that process from inserting content into an already generated view.

astra-6.text:
I think they should feel like a natural part of the world. You can use a prompt to introduce something—a change in the weather, a new object, an event—but then the interesting question is how that change interacts with everything that’s already there. If you introduce rain, you want the world to respond coherently, rather than just putting a rain effect over the image.

So there are really two ways of interacting: you’re acting within the world, and you’re also able to direct what happens in it. We want those to work together. The prompt introduces a change, and then you can keep exploring and see its consequences. That’s a much richer form of control than having to describe every frame.

r001.rationale: The response says a prompt can introduce a change or event into the world, separately from acting within it, conveying that events can be prompted rather than caused by the agent.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that prompted content may appear by looking toward another part of the world.

r003.rationale: It does not describe conditioning next-frame generation on event prompts or otherwise specify how prompts enter the generation process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they should feel like part of the world, rather than an edit pasted on top of it. If you prompt an event—say, a storm starts—the world should respond coherently. You should see changes in the environment, and those changes should affect what happens as you continue interacting.

The interesting balance is between control and surprise. You want to be able to steer the experience, but you don’t want to specify every detail. You describe what should happen, and the model fills in how it unfolds in a way that makes sense for the world you’re already in.

r001.rationale: The response gives a prompted storm as an example, but does not clearly say the event can happen independently of the agent.

r002.rationale: It describes environmental changes during continued interaction, but does not say prompted content can appear by looking toward another part of the world.

r003.rationale: It says events should feel integrated rather than pasted on, but does not describe conditioning next-frame generation.
